descripcion: Banco del diagnóstico adaptativo: 4 habilidades × 5 niveles (A1–C1) × 3 preguntas. Los textos de lectura están en 'pasajes'.

pasajes.R-A1: Hi! My name is Laura. I am 24 years old and I live in a small apartment with my cat, Max. I work in a bakery. I start work at six in the morning, so I go to bed early. On Sundays, I visit my parents.
pasajes.R-A2: Last summer, Diego travelled to Peru with two friends. They wanted to see Machu Picchu, but the train tickets were sold out, so they walked for four days on the Inca Trail. It was hard and it rained a lot, but Diego says it was the best trip of his life. Next year, he wants to visit Bolivia.
pasajes.R-B1: More and more companies are allowing employees to work from home. Supporters say remote work saves time and money, since people don't need to commute. However, some workers feel lonely and find it difficult to separate their work life from their private life. Many experts now recommend a 'hybrid' model, in which employees spend two or three days a week in the office and the rest at home.
pasajes.R-B2: Although sleep is often treated as a luxury, research consistently shows it is a biological necessity. During deep sleep, the brain clears out metabolic waste that accumulates during waking hours, and memories formed during the day are consolidated. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked not only to poorer concentration but also to a higher risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Nevertheless, in many cultures, working long hours on little sleep is still seen as a sign of dedication rather than a health risk.
pasajes.R-C1: The placebo effect has long been dismissed as a mere nuisance in clinical trials—something to be controlled for rather than understood. Yet a growing body of evidence suggests that expectation can trigger measurable physiological changes, from the release of endogenous opioids to shifts in immune response. Intriguingly, some studies report that placebos can work even when patients are told openly that they are receiving an inert pill, which undermines the assumption that deception is essential. Critics caution, however, that such 'open-label' effects are largely confined to subjective symptoms like pain and fatigue, and that enthusiasm should not outpace the data.
